clue.text: Uncertain moment not starting

indicators.note: a word that is not starting has lost its opening letter, so the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: a jiffy is a very short moment

explanation.surface: Someone hesitating at a moment when things refuse to get going.
explanation.definitionFit: Iffy is informal for doubtful or not certain, used of plans or outcomes that may not happen.

clue.text: Wish for large kind of pudding outside

indicators.note: the pudding sits outside, wrapping round the other letter

blocks.note: pease pudding is a dish of boiled split peas
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Someone hankering after a large helping of some sort of pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Pease pudding is a traditional British dish of boiled split peas. The answer is the verb in 'do as you please', meaning do as you wish.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to please means to like or choose, as in 'take whatever you please'.

clue.text: It's important to put out flame in gun

indicators.note: to be put out is to be disturbed or thrown into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A safety instruction: it matters to extinguish a flare-up inside a firearm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as extinguish, matching the flame, but it signals disorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something meaningful carries significance or consequence, which is what being important amounts to.

clue.text: Correct error about a lion, perhaps

indicators.note: an error that is corrected gets put right by rearranging what went wrong
about means going round, so the rearranged letters surround the single letter

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to fix a mistake concerning some lion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correct' looks like an adjective or a request to mark homework, but it tells you to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A roarer is any creature that bellows loudly, and a lion is the classic example, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: First man to trade in water

blocks.note: in Genesis Adam is the first man
a sale is a piece of trade

explanation.surface: The first man in history to go into business dealing in water.
explanation.walkthrough: Adam's ale is a jocular old phrase for plain water, since Adam had nothing else to drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam's ale is a humorous idiom for drinking water, the only drink available in Eden.

clue.text: Suffering keeps father at home

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Illness confines Dad to the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps' suggests a container, but the pieces simply follow one another.
explanation.definitionFit: Pain and suffering are near synonyms for physical or mental distress or hurt.

clue.text: Expert is in shape, initially every day

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word that follows it

blocks.note: in form, meaning in good shape or condition
first letter of every
D is the standard abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A specialist who keeps fit by starting each day with exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' seems to modify 'every day' as a whole, but it takes only the first letter of 'every'.
explanation.definitionFit: An informed person is well briefed and knowledgeable, close to the adjective sense of being skilled or knowing.

clue.text: Footballer deep into Trollope letters

indicators.note: the name lies buried deep inside the words that follow

blocks.note: found across the end of the novelist's name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A football star absorbed in reading the correspondence of the Victorian novelist Trollope.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelé, the Brazilian striker who won three World Cups, is often called the greatest footballer of all time.

clue.text: Lie with deceitful poet

blocks.note: false means dishonest or deceitful
Thomas Hood, the 19th-century English poet

explanation.surface: A lying, two-faced poet telling untruths.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hood wrote 'The Song of the Shirt'; setters often use him for these four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A falsehood is an untrue statement, exactly what a lie is as a noun.

clue.text: Girl hiding in a pannier

indicators.note: something hiding in a word is tucked away among its letters

blocks.note: sits inside the word for a saddlebag or basket

explanation.surface: A little girl concealing herself inside a big basket.
explanation.definitionFit: Annie is a female first name, and a clue may define any given name simply by gender.

clue.text: Desire to be paid at the end of May

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: last letter of May
to earn is to be paid for work

explanation.surface: Someone hoping their wages will arrive at the close of the month of May.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn is to long for something intensely, a strong form of wanting or craving.

clue.text: Such a feature makes Ann morose

indicators.note: makes says the letters that follow are made from something else, the other two words reworked

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A facial feature so unflattering it makes poor Ann gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer's own letters rearrange into 'Ann morose', so the clue doubles as a comment on the nose itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman nose is a facial feature, a prominent nose with a high bridge seen on Roman statues.

clue.text: Mrs Mopp is more hygienic

blocks.note: first meaning: the charwoman in the wartime BBC radio comedy ITMA
second meaning: comparative of an adjective for free of dirt

explanation.surface: A charlady keeps things more sanitary.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Mopp, a charlady in the 1940s radio show ITMA, became a byword for a household help; a charlady is a paid domestic help.
explanation.definitionFit: A charwoman is a domestic help, and as an adjective the word is the comparative of spotless or tidy.

clue.text: Chanel needs a bedtime drink

blocks.note: Coco Chanel, the French fashion designer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A famous designer wanting a warm drink before bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot chocolate made with powdered cacao is a traditional warm milky drink taken before sleep.

clue.text: A bogus journalist is full of remorse

blocks.note: taken as written
sham means fake or bogus
ED is short for editor, the crossword's stock journalist

explanation.surface: A fake reporter feels sorry for what he has done.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ashamed means feeling guilt or embarrassment over one's conduct, which is regret or contrition.

clue.text: Mad Theresa's broken beak

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, ready to be reassembled in another order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A crazed woman named Theresa has damaged her nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the letters; 'broken' does that job. Beak is British school slang for the person in charge of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: Beak is old British slang for a schoolmaster or magistrate, especially the head of a school.

clue.text: Actor to give all - nearly!

indicators.note: nearly all of something means all but its final bit, so the last letter is lost

blocks.note: to donate is to give away

explanation.surface: A plea for a performer to give everything he has, or almost.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Donat was the British film star of 'The 39 Steps' and 'Goodbye, Mr Chips'.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Donat was an Oscar-winning English film star of the 1930s, a performer of stage and screen.

clue.text: Clown seen in cold mood

blocks.note: C for cold, as on a tap
a huff is a sulky, offended mood

explanation.surface: A circus clown spotted in a frosty, sulky temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition uses an old sense of clown, meaning a boor or country bumpkin rather than a circus performer.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives chuff as a dialect word for a rustic boor, the older sense of clown meaning lout.

clue.text: I run with a fly spray, but without justice

indicators.note: a spray scatters things, so these letters are dispersed and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written
the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone chasing an insect with insecticide, an unjust end for the fly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spray' reads as a noun, the insecticide, but works as the instruction to mix the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in an unjust or inequitable manner is acting with no fairness, the adverb's plain meaning.

clue.text: Step on it to get to the rag-and-bone man

definitions.text: Step on it to get to the rag-and-bone man

blocks.note: surface reading: hurry up to catch the scrap collector

blocks.clueFragment: to get to the rag-and-bone man
blocks.note: setter's reading: tack this word on after Step and the result is the name of the famous TV scrap dealer

explanation.surface: Urging someone to hurry to catch the rag-and-bone man's cart.
explanation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son was a BBC sitcom about a father and son who were rag-and-bone men, door-to-door collectors of junk; put this word on Step to get their name.
explanation.definitionFit: The part of the foot you stand on tiptoe with completes the surname of the sitcom's scrap-dealing family.

clue.text: Drink to ITMA revival with song

indicators.note: a revival brings something back in a new form, so the radio show's letters come back reshaped

blocks.note: the letters taken as written
an aria is a song in an opera

explanation.surface: Raising a glass to a comeback of the old radio comedy ITMA, with a song.
explanation.walkthrough: ITMA, short for 'It's That Man Again', was a hugely popular BBC radio comedy of the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Tia Maria is a brand of coffee liqueur, a drink in the sense of an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Poet takes gold to hideaway

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a den is a private retreat or lair

explanation.surface: A poet carrying his treasure off to a secret retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was the Anglo-American author of 'Funeral Blues', one of the major twentieth-century writers of verse.

clue.text: Little twin boys, one demanding fodder

blocks.note: two of the short form of Alfred, side by side like twins
a, the indefinite article, means one

explanation.surface: Small twin brothers, one of them clamouring for food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little' signals a shortened name rather than small size: Alf is short for Alfred, and the twins give it twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfalfa, also called lucerne, is a leguminous plant grown as feed for cattle and horses.

clue.text: Humpback returning to King Arthur's city

indicators.note: returning means heading back the way it came, so the short word that follows is read backwards

blocks.note: a camel is the animal with a hump on its back
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hunchback travelling back to the court of the legendary British king.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian legend Camelot is the castle and court where the king held his Round Table.

clue.text: Found European leader in decrepit aircraft

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of the word is kept
in places that letter inside the other piece

blocks.note: first letter of European
crate is slang for a rickety old plane or car

explanation.surface: A European statesman discovered in a broken-down old plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' looks like the past tense of find, but it is the verb meaning to establish.
explanation.definitionFit: To found something is to establish or originate it, so it means bring into being.

clue.text: No priest set to join the human race

blocks.note: to lay is to set down
man in the sense of mankind

explanation.surface: Someone who gives up the priesthood to rejoin ordinary humanity.
explanation.definitionFit: A layman is someone not ordained, one of the laity rather than the clergy.

clue.text: I carry papers for temporary patient

blocks.note: brief means short-lived
a doctor speaks of a patient as a case

explanation.surface: A hospital worker carrying the records of a short-stay patient.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks in the first person as the object itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A briefcase is a flat bag for holding documents, so it describes itself as a carrier of papers.

clue.text: Bachelor, when half-cut, wrote many cantatas

definitions.note: describes the composer by what he did rather than naming him

indicators.note: cut by half means only the first half of the word survives

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A single man who, while tipsy, composed lots of choral works.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for drunk, which gives the surface its picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Sebastian Bach composed over two hundred surviving sacred and secular cantatas for Leipzig churches.

clue.text: Politician too fine to be promoted

indicators.note: in a down clue, promoted means moved upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
F for fine, as on pencil grades; that the letters also run backwards across these two words is a coincidence of this parse

explanation.surface: A politician deemed too good to be moved up the ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Foot was leader of Britain's Labour Party from 1980 to 1983.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Foot was a British Labour MP and party leader, a politician by profession.

clue.text: An unsupported claim conveys nothing

blocks.note: says means conveys or expresses
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A baseless assertion communicates nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's say-so is their bare word or assertion, offered without any proof or backing.

clue.text: Large trees - very large to hide a king

indicators.note: hiding something means wrapping round it, so the outer letters enclose the others

blocks.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing size
taken as written
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Huge trees big enough to conceal a monarch, as Charles II hid in one.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the Royal Oak, where Charles II hid after the Battle of Worcester.
explanation.definitionFit: Oaks are big deciduous hardwood trees of the genus Quercus, noted for their spreading size.

clue.text: String found in hole behind monk's room

indicators.note: behind places the first-named piece after the monastic room, so the round letter goes second

blocks.note: a cell is the small room a monk lives in
O is round like a hole

explanation.surface: A length of cord discovered in a gap at the back of a monastery bedroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'String' is not twine: it is a member of the string section of an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: The cello is a bowed instrument of the violin family, one of the orchestra's string section.

clue.text: Ignorant, like Blind Pew?

blocks.note: first meaning: not knowing what is going on
second meaning: unable to see, as the sightless pirate in Treasure Island

explanation.walkthrough: Blind Pew is the sightless old pirate who delivers the black spot in Stevenson's 'Treasure Island'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being kept uninformed is an idiom for lacking knowledge, and literally describes someone who cannot see.
